opus-5.5.text:
I think that claim confuses what a PhD student produces with what a PhD student is actually for. If you see a student as someone who turns ideas into code and runs experiments, then sure, agents are getting remarkably good at a lot of that. I use them myself, and things that used to take a student a week can sometimes be done in an afternoon. I don't want to downplay that. It's a real change, and it will affect how we work and possibly how we train people.

But the implementation was never the hardest part of research. The hard part is figuring out which question is worth asking, noticing that a result looks a little strange and deciding to chase it instead of dismissing it, and having the taste to know when something is interesting versus merely publishable. Agents can help with those things, but so far I haven't seen them own them. Someone still has to direct the work, judge it, and take responsibility for whether it's actually true. And agents can produce something that looks right, with a nice plot and a clean write-up, while there's a subtle bug or a flawed evaluation underneath. Catching that takes real understanding, so in some ways it raises the bar for the human.

There's also a more basic point: a big reason universities have PhD students is to train the next generation of researchers. A student isn't just labor for the advisor. If you asked, "Can an agent replace this student's output on this one project?", maybe sometimes the answer is yes. But that's the wrong question. Where do future professors, research leaders, and people who can supervise these systems come from, if nobody goes through that process of struggling with hard problems?

And my experience with students is that the ones who are good with these tools just become much more ambitious. A single student can now try many more ideas and take on projects that would have required a whole team before. So I don't see it as making students unnecessary. If anything, a strong student with agents is more powerful than ever. What may change is which skills matter most: less weight on raw implementation, more on judgment, clear thinking, and asking good questions. It's a shift in the job, and I'd take that over the idea that the job goes away.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that claim gets the picture backwards. The coding agents are very good at the part of research that was never the bottleneck. Writing a training loop, setting up a data pipeline, refactoring a messy codebase, reproducing a baseline from a paper: these used to take a first-year student weeks, and now they take an afternoon. That is real, and I don't want to minimize it. But if you ask what actually made a research project succeed or fail in my group, it was almost never the implementation. It was whether the student asked a good question, whether they noticed that a result was suspicious, whether they knew which of the fifty experiments they could run was the one worth running.

Those are taste judgments, and taste is built by doing the work, including a lot of the boring work. So there is a tension here that I think about a lot. If the agent does all the implementation, where does a student develop the intuition for what is hard, what is cheap, what tends to break? When I was a student, half of what I learned about why certain architectures work came from debugging why mine didn't. If that friction disappears, we have to be deliberate about replacing it with something.

My honest view is that the role of the student changes rather than disappears. The student becomes more like a principal investigator earlier in their career: directing agents, evaluating outputs, deciding what matters. That is harder, not easier, and it raises the bar on judgment. A student who can only execute instructions was already in a difficult position. A student who can define a problem well and tell a real finding from an artifact is more valuable now, because they can run ten times as many ideas through the system.

And I'd add one more thing. The frontier of research is, by definition, where the existing models are weakest. The agent is trained on what has been done. It is extremely good at the median of the literature. The interesting work lives in the tail, and that still requires a person who is willing to be confused for a long time about something nobody has an answer for yet. I have not seen an agent that enjoys being confused. My students, on their best days, do.

astra-6.text:
I think that claim confuses writing code with doing research. Coding is an important part of research, but the harder part is often deciding what question to ask, designing an experiment that actually answers it, and understanding what the results mean. An agent can help you implement something, but that doesn’t automatically tell you whether it was worth implementing.

For students, I think this changes what they need to learn and how they spend their time. They may be able to test ideas much faster. But they still need enough understanding to notice when an implementation is wrong or when a result doesn’t support their conclusion. Otherwise, you can produce a lot of experiments without learning very much.

And training students is itself part of the purpose of research. We’re helping people develop independent judgment. So I see coding agents as tools that can make students more capable, rather than a reason students become unnecessary.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that view confuses doing research with writing code. Coding is an important part of our work, and agents can help with that. But a research student is also deciding what question to ask, whether an experiment actually tests the idea, and what to make of a result that doesn’t fit their expectations. Even if the code works, that doesn’t mean the scientific conclusion is right.

And students are here to learn how to do those things. If we use an agent to make implementation faster, we can spend more time thinking about the problem and discussing the evidence. That can change how we train students, but I don’t see it as making students unnecessary.
